items.title: NEW: Lawmakers introduce Congressional Review Act resolutions (H.J.Res.215 / S.J.Res.213) to permanently kill the D/S-ending final rule
items.summary: On Sept 15, 2026 -- the day after Judge Saylor's preliminary injunction -- Reps. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) and Jamie Raskin (D-MD) introduced H.J.Res.215, and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-CA) introduced the Senate companion S.J.Res.213, both joint resolutions of congressional disapproval under the Congressional Review Act (CRA) targeting DHS/ICE's final rule 'Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media' -- i.e., the same rule that ends duration of status (D/S) and is the subject of the ongoing Presidents' Alliance v. DHS litigation (item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08'). Cosponsors on the Senate side include Durbin, Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Markey, Van Hollen, Wyden, Welch, King, Shaheen, Kaine, and Booker; House cosponsors include Fletcher and Liccardo. The resolutions are endorsed by AAMC, AAPPR, and 40+ other higher-ed/medical organizations. WHY THIS MATTERS for a VT student weighing an extra semester: unlike the court injunction (which only pauses the rule while litigation proceeds and could be lifted on appeal with little notice), a CRA resolution of disapproval -- if passed by both chambers and signed by the President, or enacted over a veto -- would permanently void the rule and bar DHS from issuing a 'substantially similar' replacement rule without new legislation. This is a second, independent track (alongside the litigation) that could permanently resolve the D/S uncertainty in students' favor. However, realistically: both chambers are Republican-controlled and the President would have to sign a resolution disapproving his own administration's rule, so passage is a long shot absent significant defections -- this is more a political signal and pressure tactic than a likely near-term outcome. No floor vote or committee action has been scheduled or reported as of this run.

items.title: NEW: DHS proposes eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, E, and TN workers -- shrinks the safety margin for F-1 students transitioning from OPT/STEM OPT into H-1B status
items.summary: On Sept 11, 2026, DHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (doc. 2026-18631, 91 FR 57807; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364) proposing to remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), which currently gives certain nonimmigrant workers -- H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN, plus their dependents -- up to a 60-day discretionary grace period after their employment ends and before their authorized stay expires. If finalized as written, a worker in one of these classifications (and their spouse/children) would be considered to have failed to maintain status the day after employment ends, and would be expected to depart the U.S. immediately unless separately authorized to remain (e.g., a timely new petition or change of status). This does not directly change the F-1 grace period (that is a separate, already-tracked provision of the enjoined D/S final rule -- see items above), but it is highly relevant to the same population this tracker follows: F-1 students who complete OPT or STEM OPT and transition into H-1B status. Today, an F-1 student moving to H-1B after OPT typically still benefits from the general 60-day grace period once employment ends; if this NPRM is finalized, that buffer disappears for H-1B (and the other listed classifications), meaning a layoff or employer-side delay during the OPT-to-H-1B transition could leave far less room to find new work, change status, or depart, compounding pressure on anyone already extending their program via an extra semester. Public comments are due by Nov 10, 2026; this is a proposed rule only -- it is not yet in effect and has not been challenged in litigation.

items.title: Federal court grants nationwide preliminary injunction blocking the D/S-ending final rule, one business day before its Sept 15 effective date -- DHS/ICE barred from implementing the rule while litigation continues; government expected to appeal
items.source: Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration / NAFSA (press release); press reporting
items.summary: On Sept 14, 2026 -- one day before the D/S-ending final rule's Sept 15 effective date -- U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) granted nationwide preliminary relief in Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. DHS, 1:26-cv-13799 (D. Mass.), the coalition suit filed Aug 18, 2026 by NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance, AICUM, AFT, GLO, UAW/UAW Local 2322 and The NewsGuild-CWA. The order blocks DHS and ICE from implementing the rule nationwide (not just for plaintiffs' own members) while the case proceeds, and the court reportedly wrote that 'the promulgation of the rule clearly failed to comply with the [Administrative Procedure Act],' calling the administration's stated national-security rationale weak and questioning whether the rule's real purpose was something else. As a result, F, J, and I nonimmigrants -- including F-1 students -- continue to be admitted for duration of status (D/S) for now, and the planned shift to a fixed admission period (capped at 4 years, tied to the I-20/DS-2019 program end date, requiring a separate Form I-539 extension-of-stay adjudication to go beyond it) has NOT taken effect. This is directly the scenario this tracker exists to watch: the enjoined rule is exactly the mechanism (a hard, USCIS-adjudicated admission-period cap) that would have squeezed a VT student needing an extra semester or two to finish. For now, the older, more forgiving D/S framework (extend by simply getting a new Program End Date on the I-20 from the DSO, no separate USCIS filing or adjudication needed just to keep pursuing 'normal progress') remains in place. IMPORTANT CAVEATS: (1) this is a PRELIMINARY injunction, not a final ruling -- the underlying legality of the rule has not been decided; (2) the government is widely expected to seek an emergency stay of the injunction and/or appeal to the First Circuit, and immigration counsel are advising students and employers to be prepared for the rule to be reinstated 'with little or no notice' if a higher court disagrees; (3) separately, and confusingly, USCIS and SEVP proceeded on Sept 14-15 with technical rollout tied to the now-enjoined rule anyway -- see new item 'ds-rule-operational-rollout-2026-09' -- so DSOs/students should watch for conflicting signals about which forms/processes currently apply. This tracker will keep monitoring for (a) any DHS emergency-stay motion or appeal, (b) any Federal Register notice postponing/updating the rule's status, and (c) Cranwell/VT guidance responding specifically to the injunction.

items.title: DHS Final Rule: Fixed Time Period of Admission & Extension of Stay (ends Duration of Status) for F, J, I nonimmigrants
items.summary:
STATUS UPDATE (2026-09-15): although this final rule was published in the Federal Register on July 17, 2026 and was scheduled to take effect Sept 15, 2026, a federal court granted a NATIONWIDE PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION on Sept 14, 2026 blocking DHS/ICE from implementing it while litigation proceeds -- see item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08' for full detail. As of this run, the rule's core change (ending duration of status in favor of a fixed admission period capped at 4 years) is NOT in effect; F, J, and I nonimmigrants continue to be admitted for duration of status under the pre-existing framework. This is a preliminary, not final, posture -- the rule remains validly published and could be reinstated on appeal or after further proceedings, potentially with little notice. Original rule background retained below.

DHS published a final rule (doc. 2026-14439) on Jul 17, 2026, ending open-ended Duration of Status for F-1 students, effective Sep 15, 2026. Students get a fixed 'Admit Until Date' capped at 4 years (24 months for language programs); anyone needing more time must file Form I-539 (Extension of Stay) with USCIS in addition to the existing DSO SEVIS extension -- the I-539 EOS filing fee is reported as $420 filed online / $470 by paper. A timely-filed EOS gives up to 240 days of authorized stay while pending. The rule also shortens the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 to 30 days for anyone who travels/re-enters or gets an EOS approval after the effective date. Students already in D/S status who remain continuously in the U.S. without leaving/re-entering keep transition protections, but only up to a hard outside cap of Nov 14, 2030 (4 years + 60-day grace period measured from the Sep 15, 2026 effective date). DHS has discretion to postpone, until as late as Sep 14, 2028, implementation of the specific provisions restricting mid-program school transfers, changes in educational objective (major/level), and progression to same- or lower-level programs, if DHS determines full implementation isn't feasible by the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- this discretionary postponement option applies only to those specific transfer/education-level provisions, not to the core fixed-admission-period change itself. As a major rule, it is also subject to Congressional Review Act review: Congress has a 60-day window after the rule is reported to introduce a joint resolution of disapproval, which -- if enacted -- would void the rule and bar a substantially similar rule absent new legislation; as of this run no such resolution has been reported as introduced. USCIS will publish revised editions of Form I-539 and Form I-765 effective Sep 15, 2026, aligned to the new fixed-admission-period process -- the current 08/28/24 edition of Form I-539 will still be accepted if postmarked or e-filed before Sep 15, 2026, but rejected on/after that date (no grace period), after which only the new 09/15/26 edition is accepted. On Aug 18, 2026, the anticipated legal challenge became a real lawsuit: NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, and other higher-ed/labor groups filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction against the rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (case assigned to District Judge F. Dennis Saylor, IV), seeking to stay and vacate it (or at minimum block its enforcement against plaintiffs and their members) before the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- see item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08' for full details. SEVP is hosting a live stakeholder webinar on Mon, Aug 31, 2026, 2-3pm ET to review the rule's major changes and answer FAQs. Virginia Tech's Office of the Provost and Cranwell International Center have now published VT-specific implementation guidance -- see the new item 'vt-provost-cic-guidance-2026-08' -- including a hard Aug 31, 2026 deadline for graduate students needing a program/major change or school transfer processed before the transition. NEW (2026-09-12): a GAO legal decision (B-338604, dated Aug 4, 2026) found that the rule's Sep 15, 2026 effective date does not appear to satisfy the Congressional Review Act's 60-day delay requirement for major rules, since the Senate received the rule Jul 20, 2026 (60 days would run to on/about Sep 18, 2026) -- an official, .gov-sourced procedural detail, not a court ruling, and DHS has not been reported changing its effective date as a result. The rule's effective date is now TOMORROW (Sep 15, 2026), with no DHS/SEVP announcement of any delay or postponement found. The previously-tracked discrepancy over SEVIS Release 6.89.1's deployment-window end time is now resolved in favor of Sep 14, 8:00 PM ET through Sep 15, 4:00 AM EDT, per Study in the States' own planning-guide content. Update 2026-09-18: USCIS's own I-539/I-765 pages (uscis.gov/i-539, uscis.gov/i-765) now carry a direct DHS statement confirming the rule's effective date is postponed and USCIS is proceeding under the pre-existing (D/S) framework pending further court order -- see item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08' for the full quoted text. Relatedly, USCIS has reversed the Sept 15 form-edition rollout: filers are now instructed to continue using the 08/28/24 edition of Form I-539 and the 08/21/25 edition of Form I-765, since the 09/15/26 editions are not being accepted while the injunction stands -- see item 'ds-rule-operational-rollout-2026-09' for detail. No DOJ notice of appeal or stay motion found today; no new GAO/CRA development found today.

items.title: UPDATED: USCIS reverses course -- new I-539/I-765 form editions did NOT take effect after all; filers told to keep using the old editions while the injunction stands
items.source: USCIS newsroom alert / uscis.gov form pages; ICE/SEVP broadcast message and Study in the States SEVIS Release Planning Guide
items.summary:
Two purely operational/technical rollouts tied to the now-enjoined D/S-ending final rule (see 'd-s-final-rule' and 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08') proceeded on their original Sept 14-15, 2026 schedule even though a federal court blocked the rule's substantive effect on Sept 14: (1) USCIS announced via an official newsroom alert that revised editions of Form I-539 (Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status) and Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization), both dated 09/15/26, would be published Sept 15, with no grace period -- USCIS said it will reject older editions postmarked/e-filed on or after that date; and (2) SEVP deployed SEVIS Release 6.89.1 overnight Sept 14-15 (8pm-4am EDT) adding new functionality to separately track F-1 'program extension' recommendations versus 'extension of stay' (I-539) recommendations -- functionality built specifically for the fixed-admission-period system the court just blocked. Why this matters for a VT student weighing an extra semester: with the underlying rule enjoined, F-1 students should NOT currently need to file a new-edition Form I-539 just to keep pursuing a delayed program under D/S -- but because USCIS and SEVP technical rollout went ahead anyway, there is a real near-term risk of confusing or inconsistent guidance from DSOs, USCIS adjudicators, or online form portals about which process actually applies while the injunction is in effect. Students should rely on direct guidance from their DSO (e.g., Cranwell) rather than assuming any new-edition form or SEVIS workflow they encounter this week reflects a still-effective rule.

UPDATE (2026-09-18): the confusing-signals risk flagged above has been resolved, in students' favor. USCIS has now reversed the form-edition rollout in light of the injunction: its own I-539 and I-765 pages state that filers should continue using the pre-existing editions -- the 08/28/24 edition of Form I-539 and the 08/21/25 edition of Form I-765 -- because the 09/15/26 editions built for the enjoined fixed-admission-period process are not being accepted for now. In other words, despite going live in USCIS's system Sept 14-15 as originally scheduled, the new form editions are not actually in effect while the injunction stands. A VT student should NOT file the 09/15/26-dated I-539/I-765 editions right now; use the older, pre-Sept-15 editions per USCIS's current guidance on uscis.gov/i-539 and uscis.gov/i-765. It remains unclear whether SEVP's SEVIS Release 6.89.1 functionality (the new 'program extension' vs. 'extension of stay' tracking) has also been rolled back or is simply sitting unused while D/S remains in effect; no SEVP follow-up broadcast message specifically addressing this was found today.

items.title: NEW: Virginia Tech Provost/Cranwell issue formal guidance on the D/S rule -- Aug 31, 2026 deadline for grad program/major changes and school transfers
items.source: Virginia Tech News / Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost + Cranwell International Center (official university notice)
items.summary: Virginia Tech's Office of the Provost and the Cranwell International Center (CIC) published formal guidance for VT faculty and staff on anticipated campus impacts of the Sep 15, 2026 DHS Duration-of-Status final rule (see item 'd-s-final-rule'). Key points directly relevant to a student who may need an extra semester: (1) all F-1/J-1 students will face increased external (USCIS-level) review of timely progress toward a degree, with any program extension now going through what VT describes as a more heavily monitored extension process; (2) students who complete one program after Sep 15, 2026 are barred from starting another program at the same or a lower level (e.g., master's-to-master's is out; master's-to-PhD remains allowed), matching the federal rule; (3) graduate students will be unable to transfer institutions or change programs until their current degree is completed; (4) undergraduates will be unable to transfer schools or change their declared major during their first year of study. Most actionable for students right now: Cranwell has set a hard internal deadline of Monday, Aug 31, 2026 for all paperwork requesting a program/major change, a program-level change (e.g., PhD to master's), or a school transfer -- submissions, including advisor comments, must reach CIC by that date to be processed under the current (pre-Sep-15) rules; this can run concurrently with the Graduate School's own approval process. This is the first Virginia-Tech-specific implementation guidance found since the D/S final rule was published on Jul 17, 2026; Cranwell's general 'Duration of Status Updates' page had previously said only that the university was still reviewing impacts with no VT-specific procedural guidance. New detail found today (2026-08-23), from Cranwell's own Duration of Status Updates page: extension requests are not reviewed until after the first day of classes in a student's final term, regardless of the reason for the request, and Cranwell states it will only be reviewing extension requests for students with a Fall 2026 program end date (Fall 2026 classes end Wed, Dec 9, 2026; degree conferral Wed, Dec 16, 2026) -- a student whose program end date falls later (e.g. Spring 2027 or beyond) is not yet described as eligible to have an extension request reviewed under this guidance. items.title: NEW: Local press reports sharp Virginia Tech international/PhD enrollment decline, dean attributes it to visa-policy uncertainty
items.source: WSET, WVTF/WMRA, Roanoke Times, Cardinal News (local press reporting, quoting VT Graduate School Dean Aimée Surprenant)
items.summary: Local Virginia outlets reported Aug 26-28, 2026 that Virginia Tech's Graduate School has seen a 14% drop in overall graduate enrollment since 2024, with international PhD enrollment specifically projected to fall about 30% in 2026-27 (overall PhD enrollment projected 16% lower than 2024, the lowest in six years). Graduate School Dean Aimée Surprenant attributed the decline directly to growing uncertainty around student visas as immigration restrictions have ramped up, saying federal policy changes have added significant uncertainty to whether international students will be able to complete their programs, and that students report feeling 'unsettled and concerned' about whether policies will change mid-program. This is the first VT-specific enrollment data point this tracker has found (as opposed to national projections like 'nafsa-enrollment-decline-report-2026' or the university, Illinois/Maryland court declarations in 'university-disenrollment-testimony-2026-08') and it comes directly from VT's own Graduate School leadership. It matters for a VT student weighing an extra semester because it signals the university itself is seeing and publicly acknowledging real strain in the international-student pipeline tied to exactly the kind of duration-of-status/program-completion uncertainty this tracker follows -- a wave of departures and deferrals can also affect advising capacity, cohort size, and departmental resources for students who stay. NEW (2026-09-09): the Virginia General Assembly's 2026 budget (SB30, amendment 133#1s) directs SCHEV to conduct a Virginia International Student Enrollment Impact Study, with findings due in a report to the House and Senate Education committees, the Secretary of Education, and the Governor by Dec 1, 2026 -- the first state-government-level response to this decline found by this tracker; separately, updated Cardinal News-sourced reporting puts the statewide projected tuition/fee revenue loss at approximately $23 million (fall 2025 vs. fall 2024).

items.title: UPDATED: $100K-fee OPT rule (RIN 1653-AB01) clears White House/OIRA review -- Federal Register publication now the next step
items.source: Press reporting (Forbes, Bloomberg, ICEF Monitor, The PIE News, Higher Ed Dive)
items.summary:
Multiple outlets report the administration is weighing a $100,000 fee applicable to OPT employment authorization (and by extension STEM OPT), modeled on the now-struck-down $100,000 H-1B fee proclamation. As of this run, no signed proclamation or DHS published rule/fee schedule has been reported for an OPT fee -- unlike the H-1B fee, which was signed via proclamation on Sep 19, 2025 and then struck down by Judge Sorokin on Jun 8, 2026. Note: a SEPARATE H-1B petition-fee rule (RIN 1615-AD20) cleared White House/OIRA review on Aug 19, 2026 -- this is a distinct H-1B-specific rulemaking, not an OPT fee, and should not be conflated with the reported $100K OPT fee tracked in this item. Immigration attorneys quoted say an OPT fee is unlikely to survive legal challenge absent Congressional authorization, citing that H-1B precedent. Who would pay (student/university/employer) remains unresolved; USCIS has not published regulatory language explaining the proposal, coverage, exemptions, or administration. Directly relevant to students weighing an extra semester who are also counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT to work in the U.S. afterward. New development as of 2026-08-23 (per a Fragomen client alert): DHS's related H-1B petition-fee rule (RIN 1615-AD20, a separate rulemaking, tracked for context) cleared OMB/OIRA review on Aug 19, 2026, and a proposed OPT fee rule was itself submitted to OMB for review on Aug 20, 2026, and is now under review there. Fragomen notes the contents of both proposals remain confidential until released for publication in the Federal Register, and that neither proposal was included in DHS's most recent public regulatory agenda. This moves the OPT fee from informal press-reported deliberation into the formal OMB regulatory-review pipeline, but it is still not a published rule, RIN, or fee amount confirmed by DHS/USCIS -- the reported $100,000 figure itself remains unconfirmed by any official source. New development as of 2026-08-31: Bloomberg Law ('Fee Rule for Foreign Graduate Work Program Sent to White House') and Fragomen's Beltway Buzz (Aug 28, 2026) report the proposed OPT fee rule now carries a specific Regulation Identifier Number, RIN 1653-AB01, which OIRA received for review on Aug 20, 2026; DHS has reportedly classified the rule as economically significant and noted it may have international impacts. This is the first specific RIN identified for the OPT fee proposal, distinguishing it from the separate H-1B petition-fee RIN (1615-AD20). A targeted site:reginfo.gov search for '1653-AB01' today did not surface a matching entry in search results, so the RIN remains sourced to press reporting rather than an official reginfo.gov confirmation, and the fee amount, coverage, and exemptions all remain unconfirmed. Separately (H-1B context only, not this OPT item): DHS's H-1B cap-subject petition fee is now reported at a specific $103,265 figure, and a federal appeals court has declined to stay a lower court's order vacating the earlier $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee. NEW (2026-09-14): multiple secondary sources report the proposal has now 'cleared White House review' -- i.e., OIRA's EO 12866 review has reportedly concluded -- a step closer to formal NPRM publication, though a fresh direct reginfo.gov search today still did not surface a matching public entry, so this remains unconfirmed against an official source.

UPDATE (2026-09-15): per secondary reporting (Bloomberg Law, American Bazaar, Fragomen), the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) concluded its interagency review of DHS's OPT-fee rulemaking (RIN 1653-AB01) on Sept 11, 2026, moving it a step closer to formal publication. This clears the way for DHS to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) in the Federal Register, which would be the first point at which the actual proposed fee amount, who must pay it, any exemptions, and a public-comment deadline become official. Reporting is explicit that the OIRA record itself does NOT disclose a dollar figure -- the widely-reported '$100,000' number remains sourced to media reports, not published rule text. Status remains Reported, unconfirmed pending that NPRM. UPDATE (2026-09-19): ICE submitted the proposal, titled 'Optional Practical Training Fees' (RIN 1653-AB01), to OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) for interagency review on Aug 20, 2026; OIRA completed that review on Sept 11, 2026 with a 'Consistent with Change' disposition, per Bloomberg Law's reporting on the federal regulatory record. This is a concrete procedural advance -- OIRA clearance is normally the last internal step before a proposed rule is published in the Federal Register for public comment -- but the OIRA record itself reportedly does not disclose the proposed fee amount; the widely reported '$100,000' figure still comes from media sourcing, not published rule text. Relevance to a VT student: this proposal would attach a large new fee to OPT/post-completion work authorization, which is the pathway most F-1 students planning an extra semester would eventually need to use; publication of the actual NPRM (with the real fee amount and any exemptions) could come soon. items.title: UPGRADED TO CONFIRMED: Court declarations from 15+ colleges/university systems documenting disenrollments and application drops tied to the D/S rule, now matched at exhibit level directly on the case's own CourtListener docket
items.source: Inside Higher Ed (press reporting of court declarations filed in case 1:26-cv-13799); plaintiff-hosted court filings
items.summary: Inside Higher Ed reported on Aug 24, 2026 that fifteen colleges, universities, and university systems submitted declarations as part of the preliminary-injunction record in the pending lawsuit against DHS's Duration-of-Status final rule (case 1:26-cv-13799, see item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08'), documenting that the rule is already causing concrete harm weeks before its Sep 15, 2026 effective date. Declarants include the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Chicago, University of Maryland Baltimore, and University of Maryland College Park, among others. Specific figures reported: international applicants dropped more than 25% at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (the flagship campus); at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, an administrator's declaration states 32 international students admitted for Fall 2026 have withdrawn and 14 more have deferred, just weeks before the semester starts, which the declaration describes as threatening 'concrete, immediate and irreparable' harm to the institution. UMB's declaration separately warns that a resulting decline in PhD student numbers could cost the campus its Carnegie R-1 ('very high research activity') classification, since R-1 status requires conferring at least 70 PhDs annually -- a designation tied to research funding and institutional prestige. A related Chronicle of Higher Education liveblog item cites a similar warning from the University of Maryland, College Park, of a potential 30% decline in new graduate-student enrollment.

items.title: NEW: NAFSA publishes dedicated Fall 2026 Outlook -- ~111,000 fewer international students, a 9.5% drop, 63% of institutions expect decline
items.source: NAFSA: Association of International Educators / JB International (research report, press reporting)
items.summary: A report released Aug 11, 2026 by NAFSA and research firm JB International, based on institutional responses to IIE's Spring 2026 Snapshot survey, projects fall 2026 international enrollment at U.S. colleges will fall about 9.5%, citing declining applications, visa-appointment bottlenecks, and newly restrictive immigration policy (including the D/S final rule) as converging headwinds. Inside Higher Ed's own writeup puts the projected total at roughly 1,057,000 international students enrolled in 2026-27, down from an estimated 1,169,000 in 2025-26 -- a loss of about 112,000 students, consistent with the ~111,000-112,000 range other outlets cite. Estimated economic impact: ~$3.4 billion in lost local spending and ~39,000-40,000 jobs. Inside Higher Ed's coverage adds that 63% of surveyed institutions anticipate an enrollment decline for 2026-2027 (vs. 11% expecting an increase, 26% expecting stable numbers). A CNBC report on Aug 21, 2026 corroborates the same downward enrollment trend citing tighter visa policy as a driver. This is a research/economic-impact projection rather than a new rule -- it is being tracked here as evidence of how seriously the sector expects the policy changes above to bite, which is relevant context (not itself an actionable status change) for a student weighing an extra semester. New today (2026-08-27): this projection is now corroborated by realized (not just projected) government data -- Inside Higher Ed's analysis of State Department FY2025 nonimmigrant-visa issuance statistics (the underlying monthly issuance data is published directly by the State Department at travel.state.gov) found that new student visa issuances fell about 23% in 2025 versus 2024, with India down 56.6% and China down about 34% (40,034 issuances vs. 61,075 in 2024). The 23%/56.6%/34% percentage comparisons themselves are Inside Higher Ed's/CIS.org's calculations from the official monthly data rather than a State Department-published headline figure, so this new data point is included here as further corroborating context rather than as its own separately confirmed item.

items.title: SEVP tightens CPT enforcement further -- 'every student' standard described, one institution pausing non-conforming CPT effective Sep 28, 2026
items.summary: On Aug 12, 2026, SEVP issued Broadcast Message 2608-01, 'Reminder of Liability for DSOs Regarding CPT Authorization,' to every PDSO/DSO at SEVP-certified schools. SEVP says it has observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that do not meet regulatory requirements -- specifically CPT not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum -- and is increasing scrutiny of CPT approvals; the message states DSOs should only authorize CPT where its absence 'would make the attainment of a degree an impossibility.' The message does not change the CPT regulation itself and DHS's July D/S final rule separately stated it 'does not prohibit or eliminate Day-1 CPT' and 'does not make substantive changes to CPT.' But it signals stepped-up enforcement: schools found authorizing CPT improperly risk investigation and loss of SEVP certification. Washington State University's Aug 7, 2026 international-office advisory announced ISSS there will stop approving full-time CPT during the academic year starting Spring 2027, except for programs with an explicit mandatory-internship curriculum requirement -- an early example of a university preemptively tightening its own CPT approval practices. No indication yet that Virginia Tech's Cranwell International Center has announced a similar CPT-specific change; VT's CPT page still describes standard part-time/full-time CPT eligibility rules with no dated policy update, though VT's new provost/CIC guidance (see item 'vt-provost-cic-guidance-2026-08') does not mention CPT specifically either. NEW (2026-09-07) -- VIRGINIA TECH HAS NOW RESPONDED: Cranwell's own CPT page (international.vt.edu/employment/cpt.html) now states that Cranwell has paused new CPT authorizations while it evaluates SEVP's Aug 2026 broadcast messages (BCM 2608-01 and 2608-02), with an exception for programs where practical training is a required, non-elective part of the established curriculum -- meaning it appears on the student's official graduation checklist for their major and is required of every student in that program regardless of F-1 status, per the university catalog. Students who already hold CPT authorization for the current semester are not affected by the pause. Cranwell is compiling a comprehensive list of programs/courses that meet this threshold and has asked students not to submit new CPT requests until that list is published; students with currently pending CPT requests in the IntlHokies Portal will receive individual communication about their specific case. This is the first Virginia-Tech-specific CPT policy response this tracker has found since BCM 2608-01 was issued on Aug 12, 2026. NEW (2026-08-26): SEVP issued a follow-up Broadcast Message, BCM 2608-02, on Aug 24, 2026, titled 'Guidance for Designated School Officials Regarding [CPT authorization]' -- a direct follow-up to BCM 2608-01. It sharpens the compliance test schools must apply: CPT is only permitted where the training is genuinely an integral part of an established curriculum, and SEVP flags specific patterns it has observed as noncompliant, including schools describing CPT as optional rather than integral, and schools not requiring all students in the same established curriculum to complete the same practical-training component despite the regulation requiring that consistency. The message reiterates that failure to comply can put a school's SEVP certification at risk. This does not change the underlying CPT regulation (Day-1 CPT itself remains permitted per DHS's July D/S rule), but it is a second, more detailed enforcement signal within two weeks -- underscoring that DSOs nationwide, including at Virginia Tech, are under growing federal pressure to tighten CPT authorization practices.

items.title: ICE/HSI announces nationwide OPT fraud crackdown: 10,000+ students linked to 'suspect employers'
items.source: Press reporting of ICE/HSI press conference (Acting Director Todd Lyons)
items.summary: At a May 12, 2026 press conference, Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons and Acting HSI Associate Director John Condon announced that federal investigators had identified more than 10,000 F-1/STEM OPT students linked to 'highly suspect employers' -- among the top 25 OPT-employing companies reviewed. HSI site visits across eight states (TX, VA, GA, IL, NY, NJ, NC, FL) reportedly found empty buildings, locked doors, residential addresses listed as worksites, shell companies, and offshore payroll/HR arrangements; in one Northern Texas case an employer claimed 500 OPT students but had only 3 actual employees on site. Lyons called it 'only the tip of the iceberg.' Directly relevant to any student counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT -- especially under an extended timeline -- since it signals intensified employer-level scrutiny and potential SEVIS/EAD complications for students whose employer gets flagged, even if the student did nothing wrong. The core claim is now independently confirmed: the DHS final rule's own preamble (doc. 2026-14439, Federal Register, Jul 17, 2026) cites Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons' May 12, 2026 press-conference statement that ICE 'identified more than 10,000 cases of potential fraud associated with the OPT program,' tying it directly to the rule's stated justification.

items.title: USCIS Interim Final Rule enabling mandatory electronic filing (e-Filing) -- covers I-539/I-765 among forms in scope
items.summary: USCIS published an interim final rule (91 FR 51924, doc. 2026-16313), effective Aug 11, 2026, giving USCIS authority to require mandatory electronic filing (e-filing) of certain benefit requests. The rule itself does not immediately force any specific form online -- USCIS may only mandate e-filing for a form once that form has been available for e-filing for at least 180 days, and must give at least 60 days' advance public notice before a mandate for a specific form/filing circumstance takes effect. It does not affect petitions already pending. Secondary coverage lists an initial set of roughly 22 forms USCIS is expected to phase toward mandatory e-filing, reportedly including I-129, I-130, N-400, I-90, I-131, and -- notably -- I-539 (Extension/Change of Nonimmigrant Status) and I-765 (Employment Authorization). This directly matters for F-1 students who will need to file Form I-539 for an Extension of Stay (EOS) once the Sep 15, 2026 fixed-admission-period rule takes effect, and for I-765 OPT/STEM OPT applicants: if/when USCIS issues the required 60-day notice mandating e-filing for these forms, paper filing could stop being accepted for them. Public comments on the interim final rule are open through Oct 13, 2026.

items.title: NEW: DHS proposes a $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions -- comment period closes Sept 24, 2026 -- directly relevant to F-1 students' OPT-to-H-1B transition
items.summary: On Aug 25, 2026, DHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (doc. 2026-17324) proposing a new $103,265 fee, payable at time of filing, for every H-1B cap-subject petition -- including petitions filed under the U.S. advanced-degree exemption -- in addition to all other existing fees. The fee would apply to petitions filed under both the regular 65,000 cap and the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption, but not to cap-exempt petitions, extensions, amendments, or transfers for beneficiaries already counted against the cap. Public comments were due by, and the comment period formally closed on, Sept 24, 2026; if finalized, secondary reporting indicates the fee could apply to H-1B cap-selected petitions as early as April 1, 2027, unless litigation blocks it (immigration attorneys widely expect a new legal challenge, likely arguing the fee amount is arbitrary and capricious rather than a defensible cost-recovery figure). WHY THIS MATTERS for a VT student weighing an extra semester: this does not directly change F-1 status rules, but it strikes at the same population this tracker follows -- F-1 students who complete OPT/STEM OPT and hope to transition into H-1B status. A $103,265 per-petition cost (likely borne largely by employers, who may pass on hiring risk to candidates) could sharply reduce how many employers are willing to sponsor new H-1B cap petitions for OPT/STEM-OPT graduates, potentially leaving some students with fewer post-graduation options and adding pressure either to find alternative status paths or to extend time in F-1 status (e.g., via an additional degree or program) while employer sponsorship dynamics shake out. This compounds with the already-tracked NPRM to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B/L-1/O-1/E/TN workers (item 'h1b-60day-grace-period-nprm-2026-09') -- together, the two proposals would make the OPT-to-H-1B pathway both more expensive to enter and less forgiving to exit if it doesn't work out. This is a proposed rule only; it is not yet in effect and has not (yet) been challenged in litigation.
